adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Hatay included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since October 2018 governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally; Istanbul pride was banned repeatedly (police dispersed 2015 and 2016 parades with water cannon and tear gas; on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned). The page records a February 2026 press report that the government was considering a law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a sentence of one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

adds.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
adds.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
